result.question: How can public data be used to trace what Spanish political parties actually do with their public subsidies and campaign money, and to link named politicians to hate-related conduct using only verifiable records rather than inference?
result.summary: Split along the two evidentiary chains the question needs: the money trail (what Tribunal de Cuentas itemises and in what format) and the conduct trail (what official bodies have formally ruled, per party and per named person). Add the statistical baseline, the retrieval-plus-legality layer for named judicial records, and the methodology layer showing how existing trackers label discourse defensibly.

angles.rationale: Shows how NGOs and academic coders operationalise a hateful classification with documented criteria and correction processes rather than editorial judgement.

results.title: Manifesto Project Dataset — Manifesto Coding Instructions (Handbook v5, 2021)
results.snippet: The full published codebook for coding party programmes: the unit of analysis is the 'quasi-sentence' (one political argument), assigned to one of 56/76 fixed categories with written inclusion/exclusion definitions and worked examples. This is the canonical model for a defensible classification of what a party SAYS: a pre-registered, publishable coding scheme where each label traces to a specific quoted sentence in a dated primary document, so a 'hateful' claim becomes 'this quasi-sentence was coded 608/601 under published rule X' rather than editorial judgement. Directly reusable as the schema for a per-politician/per-party discourse field, and the handbook also documents coder training and the reliability test used before a coder is allowed to produce data.

results.title: Coder Reliability and Misclassification in the Human Coding of Party Manifestos (Mikhaylov, Laver & Benoit, Political Analysis)
results.snippet: The standard critique of the Manifesto Project's own coding: measures intercoder agreement in a controlled experiment and finds misclassification is 'a serious and systemic problem', arguing the category scheme should be simplified. Essential counterweight for any tracker planning to attach a contested label to a named living politician — it quantifies how much of a discourse score is coder noise, and it is the source usually cited to justify publishing confidence intervals, double-coding a sample, and a documented correction/appeal route instead of a bare binary flag. Relevant to the LO 1/1982 honour exposure: a label defended as 'reproducible under a published codebook with measured agreement' is a far stronger position than one defended as an opinion.

results.title: About — Rainbow Map & Index (ILGA-Europe)
results.snippet: ILGA-Europe's published methodology for the annual index: 76 criteria across seven thematic categories (including a dedicated hate crime and hate speech category), each explicitly weighted to total 100 points, with the criteria set and weights disclosed and revised in consultation with member organisations and national experts, and every data point verified annually against a country-expert network before publication. This is the template for scoring an entity on rights/discourse without inference — every point is tied to a named legal or policy fact, the weighting is public and auditable, and disagreement is routed through the expert-verification cycle. Note it scores LAWS AND POLICIES per country, not individuals, which is itself the relevant design lesson: the defensible unit is a documented act, not a person's presumed attitude.

results.title: Hate Crime Data-Collection and Monitoring Mechanisms: A Practical Guide (OSCE/ODIHR)
results.snippet: ODIHR's practitioner guide, written with national experts and NGOs, setting out 'Ten Practical Steps' for recording bias-motivated incidents — including the use of bias indicators as objective, listable evidence of motive rather than an assessment of the perpetrator's mind, minimum data fields per incident, and how to handle the gap between recorded incidents and prosecuted crimes. This is the operational source for the distinction a tracker must preserve: 'incident reported', 'investigated', 'charged under art. 510 CP', 'convicted' are four different records with four different evidentiary weights, and collapsing them is the failure mode that turns a verifiable record into a defamatory claim.

results.title: Our methodology — OSCE ODIHR Hate Crime Reporting
results.snippet: Describes the verification pipeline ODIHR applies to civil-society submissions: incidents are reviewed for accuracy, followed up and clarified with the submitting organisation, and screened for conformity with the OSCE definition of hate crime (a criminal offence plus a bias motive) before appearing in the public dataset; official state-submitted figures and civil-society figures are published side by side rather than merged. A concrete, copyable correction process — a third party screens, queries and can reject a submitted record — and a precedent for showing official and NGO counts as separate series instead of a single reconciled number, which matters when comparing Interior Ministry hate-crime figures against Spanish observatorio counts.

results.title: Informe sobre Incidentes de Odio por LGTBfobia en la Comunidad de Madrid (Observatorio Madrileño contra la LGTBIfobia / Arcópoli)
results.snippet: The Spanish-language worked example: Arcópoli's observatorio report carries an explicit methodology section covering estudio de incidencia, las fuentes, los datos recogidos and el procesamiento de los datos. It states its incidence criteria openly — it records everything from minor insults upward, expressly including acts that may amount to a crime, an administrative infringement, or neither, and its collection is deliberately qualitative and standardised against the reporting format used by European organisations for the ODIHR submission, with primary sources widened via the Observatori contra l'Homofòbia de Catalunya. The three-way 'crime / administrative infringement / neither' classification is exactly the granularity a Spanish tracker needs so that a JEC sanction, a Fiscalía case and a firm conviction are never shown as the same thing.

results.title: Partidos políticos — Tribunal de Cuentas (hub de fiscalización)
results.snippet: Official entry point to the two distinct TCu audit streams the money trail depends on: (a) fiscalización de la contabilidad anual of parties receiving operating subsidies, plus donations to their linked foundations/associations, and (b) fiscalización de los procesos electorales, which verifies income/expenditure compliance and the representativeness of the contabilidad electoral rendida. Where irregularities are found the TCu proposes non-award or reduction of the electoral subsidy — a hard, citable enforcement record per party per election. Everything is published as PDF reports (buscador at tcu.es/searcher with a FIS: PARTIDOS POLÍTICOS filter); no API or bulk structured download is offered from this hub.

results.title: Informe de fiscalización nº 1.628 de las contabilidades electorales (PDF)
results.snippet: A full fiscalización report — the actual artefact that carries the granularity. These reports contain per-formation annex tables (income, ordinary/operational expense, publicity, mailings, bank credit, subvención calculated vs. claimed) and a per-party findings section listing gastos no justificados / no admitidos. This is the highest-resolution public source on what parties spent, but it is a PDF with tabular annexes: any dataset has to be built by scraping/table-extraction. Report numbers are the stable citation key (I1628, etc.) usable as a verifiable per-party record.

results.title: TCu: gastos justificados de 58 M€ en la campaña de las generales de 2023
results.snippet: Shows exactly which categories the fiscalización reports on and at what resolution: total declared campaign spend, whether any party exceeded the overall gasto electoral ceiling, and separately whether the publicidad exterior and publicidad en prensa y radio sub-ceilings (LOREG arts. 55/58) were exceeded; also 11 of 16 parties with representation qualified for the mailing subsidy, 137 million envíos electorales. Confirms mailings and outdoor/press-radio advertising are itemised categories with their own legal limits — but digital/social ads are not a separate declared category. Companion release on the 2023 local elections records 3.2 M€ of 60 M€ declared as no admitidos.

results.title: LOREG art. 130 — definición legal de gasto electoral (JEC)
results.snippet: The statutory expense taxonomy the whole audit is keyed to: letters a)–h) covering propaganda y publicidad (any form or medium), alquiler de locales for rallies, remuneración de personal no permanente, transporte y desplazamiento of candidates and party leadership, and interest on campaign credit. Determines both what parties must itemise and the ceiling arithmetic. Note that 'propaganda y publicidad… sea cual fuere la forma y el medio' folds digital/social advertising into one bucket rather than breaking it out — a structural limit on how finely digital ad spend can be traced from official filings. Reform pressure exists (a PP proposal to extend the categories to streamed rallies and comidas-mitin).

results.title: Portal de Rendición de Cuentas de los Partidos Políticos — Observatorio
results.snippet: The TCu's public-facing accountability portal, backed by the telematic filing application used for annual accounts from ejercicio 2016 onward. The Observatorio exposes compliance-level data — which parties filed, whether they filed 'en plazo' (before 30 June of the following year, per the LO de financiación), and time series of submission rates. Useful as a structured, queryable compliance signal per party, and evidence that the underlying filings are already digital; but it publishes filing status and links to reports rather than line-item expenditure, so the itemised spend still lives only in the PDFs.

results.title: Infoelectoral (Ministerio del Interior) — subvenciones estatales anuales y área de descargas
results.snippet: The complementary money-in side: Interior's Dirección General de Política Interior publishes the resoluciones fixing each party's annual state subsidy, alongside electoral-expense subsidies. Infoelectoral also runs an 'Área de descargas' / Datos Abiertos section with downloadable electoral microdata (the format is fixed-width files, for which community parsers such as JaimeObregon/infoelectoral exist). So subsidy amounts received are traceable per party from official sources, and results microdata are genuinely machine-readable — while the spending side (TCu) remains PDF-only, which is the key asymmetry for building a money-trail dataset.

results.title: Ministerio del Interior — Informe sobre la evolución de los delitos de odio en España (landing page, all editions)
results.snippet: Canonical source for angle (3). Annual series published by the Oficina Nacional contra los Delitos de Odio (ONDOD), consolidating hechos conocidos (criminal offences plus non-criminal 'incidentes') fed by the Sistema Estadístico de Criminalidad from Policía Nacional, Guardia Civil, Ertzaintza, Mossos d'Esquadra, Policía Foral and local police. Broken down by ámbito de motivación (racism/xenophobia, sexual orientation and gender identity, antisemitism, islamophobia, aporophobia, antigitanismo, ideología, disability, religion, sex/gender), penal typology, victimizaciones and province. Critically for the app: distribution is PDF only — no CSV/API on this page, so any dataset must be hand-transcribed and the transcription flagged as derived. Latest edition: 1,955 hate offences and incidents in 2024, −13.8% vs 2023, 72% esclarecidos; racism/xenophobia largest bucket at 804.

results.title: Informe sobre la evolución de los delitos de odio en España 2022 (ONDOD, full PDF)
results.snippet: The actual document to read for methodology, hosted on the ONDOD portal. Contains the dedicated statistical-methodology chapter: origin of the data, the definition and statistical counting rule for a delito de odio, and the concepts of conocidos / esclarecidos / detenidos e investigados / victimizaciones. Those definitions matter for the tracker because 'incidentes' are counted alongside crimes and a single event can generate multiple victimizaciones, so year-on-year deltas are not a clean incidence measure. Interior also notes the figures are police-recorded only; from 2025 a separate victimisation survey estimates the cifra negra, which is the honest way to say the series undercounts. Data are per-year and per-province, never per-politician and never per-party, so no row in it can support attributing an incident to a named person.

results.title: Müller & Schwarz, "From Hashtag to Hate Crime: Twitter and Antiminority Sentiment", AEJ: Applied Economics 15(3), 2023
results.snippet: The best-known attempt to move from correlation to causation between political rhetoric and hate crime, and the template for what evidentiary bar a claim like that has to clear. Uses an instrumental-variable design (Twitter's early adopters at SXSW 2007) to isolate exposure, and finds Trump's tweets about Muslims predict next-day increases in xenophobic tweets, cable-news mentions and anti-Muslim hate crimes. Companion paper 'Fanning the Flames of Hate' (JEEA 19(4)) does the same for Germany and AfD Facebook. Relevant as a boundary: the design needs exogenous variation plus geocoded incident counts, neither of which exists in Spain's PDF-only, province-level series — so a tracker can cite this literature as context but cannot replicate the inference, and must not present a spending figure next to a hate-crime figure as if it were this result.

results.title: Institute for Replication (I4R) — A Comment on "From Hashtag to Hate Crime: Twitter and Antiminority Sentiment"
results.snippet: Formal replication and robustness scrutiny of the flagship causal paper above. Directly useful for the no-causal-overclaiming requirement: it shows that even a peer-reviewed IV estimate in a top field journal is contested on specification and magnitude (the headline association of roughly a one-SD rise in Twitter usage with a ~32% rise in hate crimes is examined rather than taken as settled). Cite this when writing the tracker's methodology note to justify the weaker verb — 'occurred in the same period as', not 'caused' or 'drove'. Also underlines the shared confound both literatures flag: police-recorded hate crime moves with reporting propensity and force-level recording practice, so a rise can reflect better recording rather than more incidents.

results.title: "Climate of Hate: Similar Correlates of Far Right Electoral Support and Right-Wing Hate Crimes in Germany" (Frontiers in Psychology / PMC)
results.snippet: Comparable-EU-state evidence framed the way a defensible tracker should frame it. Finds far-right vote share and right-wing hate crime are not independent — they share correlates and covary regionally — while explicitly stopping short of claiming one produces the other, i.e. a common-cause reading is as consistent with the data as a discourse-effect reading. This is the exact epistemic posture to copy for Spain: juxtapose party performance, campaign spending and regional hate-crime counts as separately sourced series, state the shared correlates (unemployment, migrant share, prior far-right presence), and let the reader see the association without the app asserting a mechanism.

results.title: "Violence, Hate Speech, and Polarisation in Far-Right Political Influencers in Spain", Javnost – The Public 32(1), 2025
results.snippet: Spain-specific, actor-level, and methodologically the closest published analogue to what the tracker wants to do: a content analysis of six named Vox politicians plus official Vox accounts on X and Instagram across the Madrid regional election campaign, coding for hate speech, violence and polarisation. Shows the defensible pattern — a pre-registered coding scheme applied to archived, quotable posts, with the classification presented as the researchers' coding of specific utterances rather than as a standing 'hateful' label on a person. Read alongside the arXiv paper on far-right influence on campaign polarisation dynamics. Note the legal gap: academic coding is not an official finding, so under LO 1/1982 and GDPR Art. 10 the app should surface the quoted utterance and its source, and reserve the adjudicated label for JEC rulings and court judgments.

results.title: CGPJ — Publicación de las sentencias (régimen legal de CENDOJ)
results.snippet: Official CGPJ statement of the publication regime: publicity of judgments rests on art. 235 LOPJ and the CGPJ Agreement of 18 June 1997, and CENDOJ must publish resolutions in anonymised form. Decisive for the tracker design: the free CENDOJ/poderjudicial.es search returns judgments with party names stripped, so a hate-speech conviction retrieved there normally cannot itself be used to name a politician — the name must come from another verifiable source (BOE, official press note, JEC resolution, or a certification obtained as interested party).

results.title: Reglamento 1/2005 CGPJ, aspectos accesorios de las actuaciones judiciales (BOE consolidated)
results.snippet: Primary norm governing third-party access to judicial books, archives and to the text of judgments once signed and deposited. Read with art. 235 bis LOPJ it requires prior dissociation of personal data, protection of persons needing special protection and anonymity of victims. This is the legal route (and its limits) for systematically obtaining full judgment texts beyond the anonymised CENDOJ database, and it defines what an 'interesado' may lawfully receive and republish.

results.title: Datos relativos a condenas e infracciones penales en la LOPDGDD y en el RGPD (art. 10)
results.snippet: Explains Art. 10 GDPR together with art. 10 LOPDGDD: criminal-conviction data may only be processed under the control of official authority or where authorised by Union/Member State law with appropriate safeguards, and a complete register of convictions may be kept only under official authority. Directly answers whether a private tracker may lawfully maintain a per-politician database of hate-crime convictions and prosecutions — the strongest legal constraint on the whole design, and why 'Fiscalía case open' (not a final conviction) is the riskiest field of all.

results.title: STC 58/2018, de 4 de junio (derecho al olvido frente a hemeroteca digital) — BOE
results.snippet: Constitutional Court judgment applying the honour/data-protection vs. freedom-of-information balance to truthful past criminal facts held in a digital archive, ordering de-indexing of names. It sets the operative canon a tracker must satisfy: information must be veraz and relevant to public opinion formation, judged case by case, with the passage of time and the person's public relevance weighing in. A sitting politician's current record scores far better under this canon than a decades-old case, which argues for time-bounding and role-bounding any named entry.

results.title: Ley Orgánica 1/1982, de protección civil del derecho al honor (BOE, texto consolidado)
results.snippet: The civil-liability statute a named politician would sue under. Key operative parts: art. 2.1 (the protected sphere is bounded by law and by the person's own acts — public figures have a reduced sphere), art. 7 (typified intrusions, including imputation of facts or value judgments that damage reputation) and art. 8 (legitimate intrusions of relevant public interest). Determines whether attaching a 'hateful' label to a living politician is an intromisión ilegítima: reporting an adjudicated fact with attribution is defensible; an inferred label is a value judgment exposed under art. 7.

results.title: Tratamiento jurisprudencial del discurso de odio online: artículo 510 CP y colectivos más afectados (USAL)
results.snippet: Academic study that actually built an art. 510 CP case corpus out of the CENDOJ repository, showing the retrieval method is workable in practice and documenting its coverage gap: Audiencia Provincial judgments are published while most Juzgado de lo Penal first-instance sentences are not. Useful as a realistic baseline for how many hate-speech convictions are systematically discoverable at all, and for the discriminatory-motive coding categories used.

results.title: La Audiencia de Madrid archiva la causa contra el cartel electoral sobre menores no acompañados de Vox (Noticias Jurídicas)
results.snippet: Audiencia Provincial de Madrid (Sección 2ª, 19/07/2021) confirms the provisional dismissal by Juzgado de Instrucción 53 of the PSOE/Podemos/IU/Fiscalía complaints against Vox's 'menas' campaign poster: no indicia of delito de odio (art. 510) nor delito electoral, framed as 'legítima lucha ideológico-partidista' in an election. This is the single most important negative precedent for any tracker: the leading attempt to get an official Spanish finding that a party's paid campaign material constituted hate speech FAILED at both instances. A defensible tracker must therefore record the outcome (archivo) as the official finding, not the accusation — and cannot treat a filed denuncia or Fiscalía appeal as an official hate-conduct link.

results.title: La Junta Electoral ordena a Vox la retirada de la lona instalada en el centro de Madrid
results.snippet: Junta Electoral de Zona de Madrid acuerdo ordering removal of Vox's Calle de Alcalá banner (hand with Spanish-flag wristband binning the LGTBI flag and feminist symbol) within one day. Decisive nuance for the project's methodology: the board expressly ruled on LOREG art. 53 (paid commercial contracting of campaign advertising outside permitted formats), and stated it was NOT competent to rule on the content's possible illegality, leaving that to criminal courts. So JEC/JEZ acuerdos are retrievable, citable, per-party records — but they are form/procedure findings, and citing one as a discrimination finding would misstate what the body decided.

results.title: Circular 7/2019 FGE, sobre pautas para interpretar los delitos de odio del artículo 510 CP (BOE)
results.snippet: The Fiscalía General del Estado's binding interpretive doctrine for art. 510 CP, published in BOE (stable, machine-fetchable, citable by BOE id). Sets the elements prosecutors must find — closed list of motives (racist, antisemitic, antigypsyism, ideology, religion, family situation, ethnicity, race, nation, national origin, sex, sexual orientation/identity, illness, disability), the public-incitement requirement, and the wide margin given to political and electoral discourse. This is the yardstick that defines what conduct can be labelled 'hate' by an official body, and the source to cite when explaining why most political rhetoric never reaches an official finding.

results.title: Memoria de la Fiscalía General del Estado 2025 — Cap. III.10 Delitos de odio y discriminación
results.snippet: Annual chapter by the specialised hate-crime prosecutor network (Fiscal de Sala + provincial delegados), with counts of diligencias de investigación, procedimientos judiciales incoados, escritos de acusación and sentencias by discriminatory motive. Published as HTML per year (2019, 2022, 2024, 2025 chapters all reachable by predictable URL), so it is scrapable without PDF parsing. Note the limit the reports themselves flag: statistics are aggregated by motive, not by defendant identity or party affiliation — so they support trend claims, never a per-politician link.

results.title: Un juez procesa por primera vez a una concejal de Vox en ejercicio por delito de odio
results.snippet: Auto de procesamiento against a sitting Vox councillor over four years of social-media messages against migrants, LGTBI people, racialised people and people with disabilities; proceedings opened on a Compromís denuncia of April 2024. Illustrates the rare case where a named, currently-serving politician has a formal judicial act attached to hate conduct — and equally the classification trap: procesamiento is an indictment, not a conviction, so under presumption of innocence and GDPR Art. 10 a tracker can record 'processed, case open, cited auto', never 'convicted' or a 'hateful' label.

results.title: Delito de odio, inviolabilidad parlamentaria y debate político (InterJuez)
results.snippet: Judicial-authored analysis of why art. 510 prosecutions of politicians so rarely succeed: parliamentary inviolabilidad (art. 71 CE) shields statements made in the chamber, and Supreme Court/ECtHR doctrine gives heightened protection to political and electoral speech — noting the TS position that the mere use of an electoral campaign slogan does not amount to incitement under art. 510.1. Sets the realistic expected yield of the 'official findings' angle: the corpus of convictions of named politicians is very small, so the tracker's per-politician layer must be built on rulings, autos and JEC acuerdos actually issued, with the archivos recorded alongside them.

claims.claim: LOREG art. 130 defines electoral expenditure by a fixed time window: only outlays made by parties, federations, coalitions or agrupaciones from the day the election is called (convocatoria) until the proclamation of the elected count as gastos electorales — so any spending outside that window is not captured by the electoral-accounting regime and must be traced through the annual accounts instead.

claims.claim: ODIHR defines "bias indicators" as objective, observable facts rather than inferred motive, giving a documentable evidentiary standard for classifying an act as bias-motivated — the same standard a tracker could adopt to avoid inference-based labelling of politicians.
claims.quote: Bias indicators are objective facts, circumstances or patterns connected to a criminal act that, alone or in conjunction with other indicators, suggest that the offender's actions were motivated in whole or in part by bias, prejudice or hostility.

claims.claim: ODIHR explicitly recommends that hate speech and discrimination statistics be kept separate from hate crime statistics, because hate speech normally lacks a base criminal offence and mixing them distorts figures and blocks international comparison — meaning art. 510 CP hate-speech convictions must not be aggregated with Interior Ministry hate-crime counts.
claims.quote: Incidents of hate speech and discrimination do not include a base criminal offence in most countries – since the speech or discrimination would not be a crime if it did not have a bias motive – and, therefore, fall outside the hate crime monitoring definition set out in this guide. As a result, including discrimination or hate speech within hate crime data and without disaggregation distorts the statistics and hinders accurate international comparisons.

claims.claim: ODIHR states that demographic data derived from official perception rather than direct confirmation is unsuitable for publication or policy use, and that bias motivation can be recorded without recording any victim or perpetrator personal background — a data-minimisation route compatible with strict data-protection regimes.
claims.quote: Demographic information that is based on police perception should only be used for internal intelligence purposes. It is important to recognize that this type of data may be inaccurate and may use categories that are not accepted by minority groups. claims.claim: Official hate-crime statistics across the OSCE region are not comparable: in 2012 ODIHR received data from only 27 of 57 participating States, with reported annual totals ranging from below 10 to over 40,000, so cross-state comparison of Spain's Interior Ministry figures against other EU states is methodologically unsound without adjustment.
claims.quote: in 2012, ODIHR received statistics on hate crimes from only 27 out of 57 participating States, with figures ranging from below 10 to over 40,000 hate crimes.

claims.claim: Rises in recorded hate crime are, in the early stages of a measurement regime, attributable to improved reporting and police training rather than to a real increase in offences — a confound that undermines any naive correlation between political campaign discourse and reported hate-crime incidence.
claims.quote: Increases in reported crimes in the early stages of measuring hate crimes are most likely to reflect an increase in reporting by victims, not an increase in actual offences.

claims.claim: A peer-reviewed AEJ: Applied Economics paper (Müller & Schwarz 2023) establishes a causal-identification design linking political discourse volume on social media to measured hate-crime incidence: higher county-level Twitter use predicts a sizeable rise in anti-Muslim hate crimes after the 2016 US presidential primaries.
claims.quote: Using an instrumental variable strategy based on Twitter's early adopters at the South by Southwest festival in 2007, we find that higher Twitter use in a county is associated with a sizeable increase in anti-Muslim hate crimes after the 2016 presidential primaries.

claims.claim: The paper links an individual named politician's own published statements to next-day hate-crime counts, i.e. it demonstrates a verifiable-record methodology (dated politician utterances joined to dated official hate-crime records) rather than inference about the politician's beliefs.
claims.quote: Trump's tweets about Muslims predict increases in xenophobic tweets by his followers, cable news mentions of Muslims, and hate crimes on the following days.

claims.claim: The authors frame their contribution as evidence that social-media political content produces offline consequences, which is the empirical premise a tracker would need to justify juxtaposing party campaign/digital-ad spending with hate-crime statistics.
claims.quote: These results suggest that social media content can affect real-life outcomes.

claims.claim: The study's identification relies on an instrument (2007 SXSW early Twitter adopters) rather than raw correlation, which sets the methodological bar for any Spanish replication: a comparable instrument or natural experiment would be required, since Spain's Ministerio del Interior hate-crime series alone supports only correlational claims.
claims.quote: Using an instrumental variable strategy based on Twitter's early adopters at the South by Southwest festival in 2007

claims.claim: The research is US-focused (Trump, 2016 primaries, county-level US hate-crime reporting), so it provides no direct Spanish or EU evidence and cannot itself support claims about Spanish parties or politicians.
claims.quote: We study whether social media can amplify antiminority sentiment with a focus on Donald Trump's political rise.

claims.claim: Official publication and custody of Spanish court judgments is a legal competence of the CGPJ under Article 560.1.10ª LOPJ, meaning judgments (including hate-speech convictions) are published through a state body rather than only via private reporters.

claims.claim: CENDOJ, the body that runs the public judgment database, is created by Article 619 LOPJ and is headquartered in San Sebastián.

claims.claim: Across 400 German municipalities, far-right (AfD) vote share in the 2017 federal election and reported right-wing hate crimes against refugees correlate at r = 0.50 (p < 0.001) — a peer-reviewed, quantified ecological association between electoral support for a far-right party and hate-crime incidence, i.e. a template for the kind of correlation a Spanish tracker could compute rather than assert.
claims.quote: far right electoral support and right-wing crimes reported were linked substantially and positively, _r_(399) = 0.50, _p_ < 0.001

claims.claim: The authors explicitly disclaim causal interpretation of the electoral-support / hate-crime link, stating the data are correlational only — the methodological constraint any tracker linking party discourse or campaign spending to hate incidents must adopt (juxtapose, do not causally link).
claims.quote: we report correlational data that do not allow for causal inferences

claims.claim: The study is built from official government hate-crime statistics — 2,211 incidents targeting refugees, 2015–2017 — joined to official election results and municipality-level socio-structural data (unemployment, proportion of foreigners), showing that state hate-crime reporting can be geocoded to sub-national units and merged with electoral data.
claims.quote: Official hate crime statistics (2,211 incidents targeting refugees, 2015-2017)

claims.claim: Socio-structural confounders explain a substantial share of both outcomes: unemployment positively predicts both AfD vote (β = 0.26) and hate crime (β = 0.34), while proportion of foreigners negatively predicts both (β = −0.42 and −0.31), with predictors accounting for 20–24% of variance — so any Spanish party/hate-crime correlation must control for these or it is uninterpretable.
claims.quote: Unemployment positively predicted both outcomes (AfD: β = 0.26; crime: β = 0.34)

claims.claim: The direction of the foreigner-share effect reverses by region — non-significant for West German hate crime but significantly positive in East Germany — demonstrating that pooled national correlations mask regional heterogeneity, relevant to any Spain-wide comparison across autonomous communities.
claims.quote: in East Germany it showed "significantly and positively" correlation with crime rates

claims.claim: Reglamento 1/2005 CGPJ Article 7 requires that judicial resolutions sent to CENDOJ be handled with dissociation of personal data, subject to data-protection legislation and articles 234 and 266 of the LOPJ — meaning CENDOJ's public jurisprudence database is anonymised by rule, so it cannot be used as a source of named-politician conviction records.
claims.quote: legislación en materia de protección de datos personales y en los artículos 234 y 266 de la LOPJ

claims.claim: Article 4 permits restricting access to judicial decisions where release would affect the right to privacy, rights of persons deserving special protection, or the anonymity of victims — a discretionary limit that applies to requests for identified individuals' judgments.
claims.quote: derecho a la intimidad, a los derechos de las personas dignos de especial tutela

claims.claim: Access to a sentencia by a non-party requires the Secretario Judicial to assess whether the requester has justified a direct personal interest, so systematic bulk retrieval of named individuals' judgments through this route is not available as an open-data channel.
claims.quote: interés personal y directo

claims.claim: All courts are obliged to remit copies of their sentences to CENDOJ, which must guarantee their integrity, authenticity and access, establishing CENDOJ as the single centralised corpus of Spanish case law available for programmatic search (albeit anonymised).
claims.quote: integridad, autenticidad y acceso

claims.claim: Article 3 fixes the moment a decision becomes accessible to interested parties: once extended and signed by the judge or all magistrates and deposited in the judicial office and registered in the IT systems — giving a defined, checkable point at which a judgment against a politician becomes retrievable.

claims.claim: The underlying study the replication verifies is explicitly about political discourse, not just general social media: it studies anti-Muslim hate crimes in relation to Twitter usage during Donald Trump's political rise, which is the closest published analogue to linking a party's campaign discourse to reported hate-crime incidence.
claims.quote: Karsten Müller and Carlo Schwarz (2022) investigate the impact of Twitter on anti-Muslim hate crimes, demonstrating that higher Twitter usage correlates with increased hate crimes, particularly during Donald Trump's political rise.

claims.claim: The replication's extended analyses show the discourse-to-hate-crime effect is heterogeneous by geography — significantly stronger in urban than rural areas — meaning any Spanish adaptation of this method would need sub-national (province/municipality) hate-crime and exposure data rather than national aggregates.

claims.claim: Under Spanish law (art. 10 LOPDGDD, LO 3/2018), processing of personal data on criminal convictions and offences — including related proceedings and precautionary/security measures — is lawful only when covered by EU law, the LOPDGDD or other legal norms, or when carried out under the supervision of public authorities; a private tracker publishing named politicians' conviction data has no general legal basis.
claims.quote: El tratamiento de datos personales relativos a condenas e infracciones penales, así como a procedimientos y medidas cautelares y de seguridad conexas...

claims.claim: The only private actors Spanish law authorises to process criminal-conviction data are abogados and procuradores, and only to collect information supplied by their own clients for the exercise of their professional functions — an exemption that does not extend to journalists, NGOs or civic data projects.
claims.quote: solo serán posibles cuando sean llevados a cabo por abogados y procuradores y tengan por objeto recoger la información facilitada por sus clientes para el ejercicio de sus funciones

claims.claim: Spanish law permits only a single complete register of criminal convictions, held under the control of the public authorities — so compiling a comprehensive per-politician conviction database outside official control is itself unlawful, independent of whether each individual judgment is public.
claims.quote: Solo podrá llevarse un registro completo de condenas penales bajo el control de las autoridades públicas

claims.claim: The official Spanish registry infrastructure for this data is the system of registros administrativos de apoyo a la Administración de Justicia, regulated by Real Decreto 95/2009 and modified by Real Decreto 913/2024 — identifying the concrete legal instrument governing access to conviction records.
claims.quote: The administrative justice support registry system (regulated by Royal Decree 95/2009, modified by RD 913/2024) governs official records

claims.claim: GDPR Art. 10 conditions any such processing on either official-authority supervision or Member State law providing appropriate safeguards for data subjects' rights and freedoms, meaning a Spanish tracker must point to a specific enabling norm plus safeguards rather than rely on public interest alone.
claims.quote: supervision of public authorities or where authorized by Union or Member State law

claims.claim: Spain's Constitutional Court, in STC 58/2018 (ECLI:ES:TC:2018:58, 4 June 2018), recognised the "derecho al olvido" as a fundamental right derived from data protection under art. 18.4 CE — establishing a constitutional basis on which an individual named in an archived report of past criminal proceedings can demand de-indexing.
claims.quote: el denominado jurisprudencialmente «derecho al olvido»

claims.claim: The ruling makes the lawfulness of continuing to publish a named individual's past judicial record depend jointly on the subject matter and on the person's status, so a public figure such as a serving politician retains far weaker olvido protection than a private individual — the doctrinal hook a tracker would rely on to publish named politicians' convictions.
claims.quote: la relevancia pública de la información viene determinada tanto por la materia de la misma como por la condición de la persona

claims.claim: The Court balanced arts. 18.1 (honour/intimidad, the LO 1/1982 sphere) and 18.4 CE against art. 20.1 d) CE (freedom of information) and granted amparo only partially against Ediciones El País — upholding de-indexing from general search engines while reversing the ban on internal newspaper-archive search, i.e. removal of a name from the underlying record was held to burden press freedom excessively.
claims.quote: prohibición de indexación de nombres y apellidos como medida

claims.claim: The harm the Court treated as decisive was retrievability of the person by name via a general search engine, not the existence of the archived record itself — implying that a politician-tracking database is exposed less by holding judicial records than by making them name-searchable and indexable to the open web.
claims.quote: mediante una simple consulta en un buscador generalista

claims.claim: The judgment concerns a digital press archive (hemeroteca digital) rather than an official judicial database, so it constrains republication of press reports of proceedings and does not itself settle the separate regime governing CENDOJ/CGPJ jurisprudence data or GDPR Art. 10 criminal-conviction processing.
claims.quote: información contenida en una hemeroteca digital

claims.claim: The Comparative/Manifesto Project's published dataset contains systemic coding error: nearly every manifesto in it was coded a single time by a single coder, with no second-coder verification, so no per-document reliability statistic exists for the gold-standard data researchers rely on.

claims.claim: Mikhaylov, Laver and Benoit ran a coding experiment in which trained human coders re-coded sample manifestos and compared the results against the published CMP codings, and concluded that misclassification is not occasional noise but a systemic property of the dataset.

claims.claim: The measured misclassification propagates into the CMP's headline derived measure — its left-right (RILE) policy scale — meaning downstream position estimates built on hand-coded categories inherit quantifiable error rather than being treated as exact.

claims.claim: The authors' remedy is scheme simplification: they argue the coding category set itself is too fine-grained to be applied reliably by human coders, so reducing category count is the fix for reliability, rather than more coder training alone.
claims.quote: CMP scheme should be significantly simplified to address reliability issues

claims.claim: The article is a peer-reviewed methods paper in Political Analysis, Volume 20, Issue 1, pages 78-91, print year 2012, providing a citable published standard for reporting coder reliability and category-level misclassification matrices in political text classification.
claims.quote: Volume: 20 | Issue: 1 | Pages: 78-91 | Print Publication Year: 2012

result.evidence:
Quote supports only "tcu.es/es/partidos-politicos/ links to cuentaspartidospoliticos.es". Everything after that is overreach and factually wrong on two counts.

(1) Submission does NOT happen on cuentaspartidospoliticos.es. It happens on the Tribunal's Sede Electrónica, sede.tcu.es/es/sede-electronica/GRCuentas/PartidosPoliticos ("Rendición de Cuentas de los Partidos Políticos"), which cites the "Instrucción que regula la presentación telemática de las cuentas anuales consolidadas de los partidos políticos" (Resolución 19 enero 2022). cuentaspartidospoliticos.es itself links OUT to that sede URL under "Saber más". sede.tcu.es is a tcu.es subdomain, not a "second domain".

(2) The substantive spending data IS hosted on tcu.es. https://www.tcu.es/es/partidos-politicos/Informes/ serves the fiscalización PDFs directly from tcu.es infrastructure at paths like /export/sites/portal/repositorio2/INFORME/<year>/<n>.pdf — e.g. "Informe de Fiscalización de las Elecciones a Cortes Generales de 28 de abril de 2019", "Informe de Fiscalización de las contabilidades de las elecciones locales de 28 de mayo de 2023". Same page tree also has /Observatorio and /Sanciones. So a scraping pipeline for electoral/annual spending must target tcu.es, the opposite of the claim.

What cuentaspartidospoliticos.es actually is: a public dissemination portal (Observatorio de rendición — whether a party filed, aggregate filing levels — plus noticias, FAQ, publicaciones). Useful as a supplement, not a required substitute. Neither domain exposes an API or machine-readable dataset of itemised expense categories, so the claim's practical implication ("target that second domain") would misdirect the pipeline.

Verdict: unsupported by the quote and contradicted by the primary sources.

The word "sole" is directly contradicted by the governing statute. Ley Orgánica 8/2007, art. 16.Uno (consolidated text, BOE-A-2007-13022, version of 30/05/2024) reads: "Corresponde en exclusiva al Tribunal de Cuentas el control de la actividad económico-financiera de los partidos políticos, SIN PERJUICIO DE LAS COMPETENCIAS RELATIVAS A LA FISCALIZACIÓN DE LOS PROCESOS ELECTORALES AUTONÓMICOS ATRIBUIDAS A LOS ÓRGANOS DE CONTROL EXTERNO DE LAS COMUNIDADES AUTÓNOMAS PREVISTOS EN SUS RESPECTIVOS ESTATUTOS." The claim quotes the tcu.es marketing/summary page, which omits the statutory carve-out. That carve-out is operative, not theoretical: regional OCEX audit party electoral accounts for their own elections and can propose reducing or withholding the subsidy — e.g. Sindicatura de Comptes de Catalunya approved the instrucción to fiscalizar the 12-M 2024 Parlament electoral accounts (sindicatura.cat) and reported on mailing spending; Sindicatura de Cuentas del Principado de Asturias does the same for Junta General elections (sindicastur.es, "Contabilidad electoral"); both publish instructions via the Junta Electoral Central (juntaelectoralcentral.es/.../sindicatura_cuentas_22042024.pdf). So for autonomous-community campaigns the TCu is NOT the auditing body and its reports do not contain that money trail.

Second overreach: "single authoritative source for a party money trail" is an inference the quote does not make. TCu fiscalización covers registered parties (and, since LO 3/2015, their linked foundations), but not: subsidies to parliamentary groups in the Cortes and regional chambers (audited by the chambers themselves), grupos políticos municipales, the actual disbursement records held by Ministerio del Interior/Congreso, or Junta Electoral Central decisions on advances and campaign content. Also relevant to the research question: TCu output is PDF reports at sede.tcu.es, itemised only at coarse expense categories — calling it "the" money trail overstates its granularity as well as its exclusivity.

The narrow reading — TCu is the exclusive external auditor of party economic-financial activity at state level — is supported. The claim as written ("sole body", "single authoritative source") is not.

Claim has two halves; the first is trivially true, the operative second half is contradicted.

TRUE PART: cuentaspartidospoliticos.es exists and is the telematic submission channel. TCU approved an Instrucción (30 March 2017) regulating "remisión telemática de las contabilidades anuales de los partidos políticos", and the platform (https://www.cuentaspartidospoliticos.es/CuentasPartidos/home) is a login-gated app ("Darse de alta" / "Área privada", usuario+contraseña) for filings from ejercicio 2016 onward.

OVERREACH vs THE QUOTE: the supporting quote is nothing but a hyperlink on tcu.es. It says nothing about where datasets live, nor that a pipeline "must target that second domain". That is inference, not what the source states.

CONTRADICTED BY PRIMARY SOURCES: the actual fiscalización output — the reports containing itemised electoral and annual party spending — is hosted ON tcu.es, not on the second domain:
- https://tcu.es/es/partidos-politicos/Informes/ ("El Pleno aprueba los informes de fiscalización correspondientes a las cuentas anuales de los partidos y a los procesos electorales")
- https://www.tcu.es/es/partidos-politicos/Sanciones and https://www.tcu.es/es/potestad_sancionadora/index.html (sanctions data)
- https://www.tcu.es/searcher/document/DocumentSearch.action?docCheckFisSelect=FIS:+PARTIDOS+POLÍTICOS (document searcher on tcu.es)

Fetching cuentaspartidospoliticos.es/es/saber-mas/ confirms the reverse direction of the claim: that portal "links externally to tcu.es" for fiscalización, pointing at sede.tcu.es, and "does not host the actual expenditure data or detailed audit findings". Its only public data layer is the Observatorio — whether a given party/fundación filed, plus aggregate compliance levels (e.g. "347 partidos políticos y fundaciones presentan en tiempo y forma las cuentas del año 2021") — not itemised gastos electorales.

So the practical instruction embedded in the claim is backwards for a scraping/dataset pipeline: the itemised-spending PDFs must be pulled from tcu.es; cuentaspartidospoliticos.es yields only filing-compliance metadata and is otherwise credential-gated (and scraping a login-gated filing portal is not an option anyway). At best the second domain is a supplementary source for "did X file", never the required target.

Claim overreaches its own quote and is contradicted by the governing statute.

1) Quote does not say "sole". The tcu.es sentence only says "corresponde al Tribunal de Cuentas la fiscalización de la actividad económico-financiera de los partidos... inscritos en el Registro". "Sole body" and "single authoritative source for a party money trail" are the reviewer's additions, not the source's words.

2) Statutory exclusivity is expressly qualified. LO 8/2007 art. 16 (as amended by LO 3/2015) grants the TdC exclusive external control "sin perjuicio de las competencias relativas a la fiscalización de los procesos electorales autonómicos atribuidas a los órganos de fiscalización externa de las Comunidades Autónomas" (BOE-A-2007-13022 consolidado). In practice, campaign spending for autonomic elections is audited by the CCAA bodies — Sindicatura de Comptes de Catalunya/València, Cámara de Cuentas de Andalucía/Madrid, Consello de Contas, Audiencia de Cuentas de Canarias — and only falls to the TdC where no such body exists. TdC's own Castilla-La Mancha 2019 electoral fiscalización exists precisely because that CCAA lacks an OCEX. So the TdC is not the sole auditor, and for regional campaigns it is often not the auditor at all.

3) A major public-money channel to parties sits outside TdC competence entirely. LO 8/2007's disposición adicional leaves accountability for subsidies to Grupos Parlamentarios (Cortes Generales, autonomic assemblies, Juntas Generales, local groups) to "lo que dispongan sus respectivos Reglamentos o normativa local específica" — fiscalised by the granting institutions, not the TdC. The TdC itself has publicly demanded action on "sobrefinanciación de los partidos a través de sus grupos parlamentarios" (eldiario.es, reporting TdC), i.e. it flags money it cannot itself audit. A "single authoritative source for a party money trail" that structurally omits parliamentary-group funding is not single or complete.

4) Other independent official records carry party money data: parties' own art. 14 publication duty (annual accounts on their websites; donations/legacies >25,000 EUR published with donor identity), Ministerio del Interior subsidy payments, JEC/LOREG electoral-subsidy advances and administrator filings, and CCAA transparency portals. TdC reports also lag years and only cover parties that receive subsidies.

Verdict: the strong half of the claim ("sole", "single authoritative source") is unsupported by the quote and contradicted by the statute's own proviso plus the parliamentary-group carve-out. Only the weak half ("TdC audits registered parties' public and private resources") survives.

result.evidence:
Overreach on two words the quote does not contain: "sole" and "single authoritative source".

1) The quote is only a competence attribution ("corresponde al Tribunal de Cuentas la fiscalización de la actividad económico-financiera de los partidos políticos inscritos en el Registro..."). It contains no exclusivity language. The claim silently upgrades it to "sole body with legal competence".

2) The actual exclusivity clause lives elsewhere — LO 8/2007 art. 16.1 (BOE-A-2007-13022, consolidated) — and it explicitly carves out other bodies: "Corresponde en exclusiva al Tribunal de Cuentas el control de la actividad económico-financiera de los partidos políticos, sin perjuicio de las competencias relativas a la fiscalización de los procesos electorales autonómicos atribuidas a los órganos de control externo de las Comunidades Autónomas previstos en sus respectivos estatutos." So for regional-election campaign money — a large slice of Spanish party spending — the competent auditor is the regional OCEX, not the Tribunal de Cuentas. Concrete instances: Sindicatura de Comptes de Catalunya approved the fiscalization instruction for the 12-M Parliament election accounts (sindicatura.cat); Sindicatura de Comptes de la Comunitat Valenciana reported on Corts campaign spending (2023); Sindicastur publishes "contabilidad electoral" for Asturias. Autonomic electoral accounting for Aragón, Asturias, Canarias, Baleares, Madrid, C. Valenciana and Navarra is handled by their own external control bodies.

3) "Single authoritative source for a party money trail" is a research-design conclusion, not a legal fact, and it is false in practice. Other verifiable public money-trail records exist and are not TCu products: parties' own mandated web publication of accounts (LO 8/2007 art. 14.8 + Ley 19/2013), municipal group allocations — which the Tribunal itself criticized in April 2025 for "significant deficiencies and insufficiencies" in their regulation and control, i.e. a flow it does not effectively audit — and criminal judgments (Gürtel/Bárcenas) that established party financing facts the TCu audits never surfaced.

4) Practical authority is further weakened by lag: reporting on multi-year delays (e.g. the 2017 report still being the latest approved in 2022, prior five-year delays) means sanctions can prescribe before irregularities are published. GRECO has repeatedly flagged the regime's incompleteness (linked foundations/associations as parallel channels).

Bottom line: the underlying gist — TCu is the central/primary party auditor — is sound, but the claim as written is contradicted by the very statute that grants the exclusivity, and its "single authoritative source" framing is unsupported by the cited quote.
